learnings.title: Acceldata in one page — what they sell, and the words to use
learnings.source: acceldata.io, newsroom, Everest/GigaOm analyst pages — researched 2026-09-12
learnings.answer:
The recruiter asked you to know the products and the investors. This is that, plus the naming traps.

## The one thing to know first

On **19 May 2026 — four months ago** — Acceldata relaunched as a unified **"Autonomous Data & AI Platform"** built on an architecture they call **xLake**. CEO Rohit Choudhary's framing:

> "The lakehouse architecture was built for human access. It broke in the agentic era."

That rebrand is recent enough that it is almost certainly what the hiring manager wants you to have noticed. Leading with it signals you looked at the company this month, not at a two-year-old summary.

## The product lines

| Line | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Data & AI Observability** | The core. End-to-end visibility over pipelines, data quality, anomaly detection, reconciliation, lineage — extended to AI agents and LLM tracing |
| **Agentic Data Management (ADM)** | Autonomous agents that detect, diagnose and resolve data issues — quality, pipeline ops, catalog, incident response. GA'd around Aug 2025 |
| **Agentic Data Engineering (ADE)** | Pipelines that "self-build, self-heal and self-optimise" — pipeline creation, federated querying, job management |
| **Data Warehousing** | A unified analytical runtime, Velox-accelerated |
| **Agentic Runtime** | The governed execution layer agents run on — distributed training, inference, GPU notebooks |
| **Open Data Platform** | Hadoop modernisation |

## ⚠️ Naming traps — read this twice

This is the part that can actually cost you.

- **Do not say "Torch."** It was the data-reliability product; today it survives only in legacy documentation URLs, not as customer-facing branding. Saying it dates you by three years.
- **Do not say "Flow."** No current product page, docs or press uses it. The pipeline story is **Agentic Data Engineering** now.
- **"Pulse" is still live but narrow** — it is specifically Hadoop observability and cost optimisation, a paid add-on to the Open Data Platform. Correct to mention only in that context; wrong as a name for their general observability product.
- **"ADOC"** (Acceldata Data Observability Cloud) is still the product-level name under the **Data & AI Observability** capability. Notably, the May 2026 launch release does not name Torch, Pulse, Flow *or* ADOC — they are moving to capability-based naming.

**Safe vocabulary:** *Data & AI Observability*, *Agentic Data Management*, *Agentic Data Engineering*, *Data Warehousing*, *Agentic Runtime*, *Open Data Platform*. Use *ADOC* if you want the product-level name, and *Pulse* only for the Hadoop angle.

## The autonomous loop

Marketing describes an **"agentic brain"** running an autonomous loop: **observe → detect → diagnose → act**, with audit trails over what the agents did.

> ⚠️ A five-stage version ending in "verify" circulates, but the site copy confirms only the four stages plus audit-trail language. Say "observe, detect, diagnose, act — with an audit trail" and you are on solid ground.

What is concretely shipping, as opposed to positioning: ADM at GA, and the comparison page's claim of **10 pre-built autonomous agents** covering data quality, pipeline ops, reconciliation and incident management.

## Customers and market

- **PhonePe** is the flagship reference — scaled monitored infrastructure from 70 to 1,500+ nodes (~2000%) and saved $5M, using Pulse for HBase/Spark/Kafka.
- **PubMatic** has a published case study. An anonymised "top national consumer bank" cut SLA breaches 96% and avoided $10M+ in fines.
- **"6 of top 12 banks," "3 of top 7 life sciences"** — these come from Acceldata's own competitive page. Fine to repeat, but attribute them ("their comparison page claims…") rather than stating them as audited fact.
- Verticals: financial services, life sciences, retail/CPG, telecom, technology.
- **Deployment is hybrid by design** — cloud, on-prem, hybrid and sovereign. This is their headline differentiator against Monte Carlo, who are SaaS-only. It matters to you: it implies on-prem builds, air-gapped environments and versioned frontend deployments.

## Analyst standing

- **Leader**, Everest Group Data Observability PEAK Matrix 2025
- **Leader and Fast Mover**, GigaOm Radar for Data Observability v3
- Data Quality Leader, G2 Fall 2024 (4.5/5)
- Forbes America's Best Startup Employers 2025

> ⚠️ Do **not** claim a Gartner Magic Quadrant or Forrester Wave placement — neither is confirmed for data observability. Everest and GigaOm are the safe citations.

## The bit that connects to you

Acceldata is roughly 300 people, four months past a full agentic rebrand, selling autonomous agents that take actions against production data and need to show a human what they did and why.

You are currently building an agent system where deterministic Go makes every rule-based decision, the model is confined to a single judgement step, and the output is a structured contract — verdict, confidence, per-field severity — that drives a reviewer console with accept / correct / escalate actions.

That is the same problem: **an agent acted, and a human has to be able to trust, audit and override it.** Do not oversell the parallel, but do not miss it either. See [The verification agent](/acceldata-prep/9).

- Funding, investors, competitors: [Funding, founders, competitors](/acceldata-prep/2)
- How this compares to Atlan: [Atlan vs Acceldata](/acceldata-prep/3)

learnings.title: Funding, founders, competitors — the facts, with the traps marked
learnings.source: PR Newswire, TechCrunch, Insight Partners, acceldata.io newsroom — researched 2026-09-12
learnings.answer:
The recruiter explicitly said to know the investors. Here is the verified version, and — more usefully — the places where the commonly-repeated version is wrong.

## Funding history

| Round | Date | Amount | Lead | Also participating |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Series A | 15 Oct 2020 | **$8.5M** | Sorenson Ventures | Lightspeed, Emergent Ventures |
| Series B | 28 Sep 2021 | **$35M** | Insight Partners | March Capital *(new)*, Lightspeed, Sorenson, Emergent |
| Series C | 8 Feb 2023 | **$50M** | March Capital | Sanabil Investments, Industry Ventures, Insight Partners |
| Series C extension | 10 Oct 2023 | **$10M** | Prosperity7 Ventures *(new)* | — |

**Named total: $103.5M.** Aggregators report ~$106M across 5 rounds, which implies an earlier seed of roughly $2.5M that is not separately documented. If you cite a figure, say **"over $100M"** — it is what the company itself said in 2023 and it cannot be wrong.

**There has been no new round since October 2023.** If asked whether they have raised recently, the accurate answer is no — everything in 2024–2026 is product, GA, leadership and analyst news. This is worth knowing: a company three years past its last raise, 300 people, having just bet the brand on an agentic relaunch, is a company with a specific kind of urgency. Do not say that out loud, but let it inform what you ask.

## The acquisition that explains the pivot

**Bewgle, 19 Sept 2023** — an AI startup founded by ex-Googlers, specialising in unstructured data (text, image, audio), acquired explicitly to extend observability into AI and LLM pipelines.

That is the root of today's "Data & AI Observability" and the whole agentic direction. Being able to trace the pivot back to a 2023 acquisition rather than treating it as 2026 marketing is a genuinely differentiating thing to know.

## Founders and leadership

| Person | Role | Background |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Rohit Choudhary** | Co-founder & CEO | Director of Engineering at **Hortonworks** — led Dataplane Services, Ambari, Zeppelin |
| **Ashwin Rajeeva** | Co-founder & CTO | Software Architect at Hortonworks, led DataPlane hybrid cloud data services |
| **Raghu Kandikonda** | Co-founder & VP Engineering | — |
| **Gaurav Nagar** | Co-founder & Senior Architect | — |
| **Gaj Hegde** | VP Engineering *(joined Dec 2021)* | Yahoo, WebEx, Google; VP/GM at Hortonworks and [24]7.ai |

The **Hortonworks lineage is the founding story** — Choudhary and Rajeeva met there. It is repeated consistently across every source, so it is safe to reference, and it explains the Hadoop/Open Data Platform line that otherwise looks like a legacy oddity next to the agentic messaging.

Later execs: Mike McQuaid (CRO), Mahesh Kumar (CMO, ex-GitLab), Ramon Chen (CPO, ex-Reltio) — all Oct 2023.

> ⚠️ No named Bangalore-based engineering leader could be found. HQ is Campbell, CA; the Bangalore office is in HSR Layout, 3rd Sector. **Who owns frontend architecture in Bangalore is a genuinely open question — and a good one to ask him.**

## Competitors

The only comparison page Acceldata authors themselves is against **Monte Carlo**. Their claimed differentiators:

- hybrid / on-prem / sovereign vs. Monte Carlo's cloud-only
- full data lifecycle, landing → consumption, vs. "consumption zone only"
- infrastructure and cost monitoring (YARN, compute) that Monte Carlo lacks
- production Kafka support vs. Monte Carlo's beta
- custom rules in SQL **plus** Python/Scala/Java/JS, vs. SQL-only
- "10 pre-built AI agents" vs. "task-based agents only"
- a claimed **38×** reduction in bad-data cost from detecting at source ("shift-left")

The rest of the field — **Bigeye** (SLA enforcement), **Soda** (open-source, rule-based, smaller teams), **Databand** (IBM), **Anomalo**, **Metaplane**, plus **Databricks and Snowflake native observability** — appears in third-party roundups, not in Acceldata's own materials. Reference them as the category, not as positions Acceldata has taken.

## The frontend stack, from their own job posting

The Bangalore senior frontend req is informative, and slightly surprising:

- **HTML, CSS, SCSS, JavaScript, React/Angular**, TypeScript
- **Webpack**, **Bootstrap**
- Redux / Flux / Context API
- **Jest**
- Git/GitLab, **Jenkins**
- Data-layer adjacency expected: RDBMS, MongoDB, **Elasticsearch**
- Band: 5–8 years; ₹20–45L plus ESOP
- Scope: *"shared front-end components across all products"*

Two things to notice. First, **"React/Angular"** appearing together across multiple postings strongly suggests a codebase split across two frameworks — very likely legacy ADOC/Pulse UI versus newer ADM/ADE surfaces. Second, this is a **Webpack/Bootstrap/Jest** shop, not a Vite/Tailwind/Vitest one. Your Elasticsearch exposure from the Atlan catalog work is directly relevant and worth mentioning.

Neither point is a problem. Both are excellent questions — see [Why Acceldata, growth expectations, and what to ask him](/acceldata-prep/14).

learnings.title: Atlan vs Acceldata — adjacent, not the same (and why saying so helps you)
learnings.answer:
On the call the recruiter said the domain is the same — *"Atlan, Databricks, Acceldata, Cloudera… the domain waves, it remains the same."* And you agreed.

He is directionally right and precisely wrong, and the difference is worth holding onto. A candidate who says *"same space, and here's exactly where the line sits"* reads as someone who understands the market. A candidate who just agrees reads as someone being agreeable.

## The actual distinction

Both sell into the enterprise data estate. They answer different questions.

| | **Atlan** | **Acceldata** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core question | *What data do we have, who owns it, what does it mean, who may touch it?* | *Is the data correct, is the pipeline healthy, what is it costing, did it break?* |
| Category | Metadata / catalog / governance — "the context layer" | Data observability and reliability |
| Buyer | Data governance leads, stewards, CDO org | Data platform / engineering / ops teams |
| Unit of work | An **asset** — a table, term, glossary, data product — and its metadata | A **pipeline run, a check, a metric, an incident** |
| Failure it prevents | Someone uses the wrong dataset, or accesses data they shouldn't | A dashboard silently shows stale or wrong numbers |
| Time axis | Mostly static state with an approval history | Continuous time series — freshness, volume, drift |

The compressed version, if you need one sentence:

> "Atlan is the catalog and governance layer — what exists, who owns it, who gets access. Acceldata is the reliability layer — is it fresh, is it correct, did the pipeline break, what's it costing. Both are trust in data; Atlan is trust in its *meaning*, Acceldata is trust in its *state*."

## Where they genuinely overlap

Be precise here, because this is where your experience actually transfers.

- **Lineage.** Both build it. Atlan uses it for impact analysis and context; Acceldata uses it to trace an incident to its source.
- **Data quality.** This is the real overlap. Atlan surfaces quality signals as asset metadata; Acceldata *is* the quality engine. Acceldata's **xGovern** component (unified catalog and asset management) is the point where they move onto Atlan's ground.
- **Both are now agent-first.** Atlan shipped **Context Agents Studio** — AI generating descriptions, READMEs and SQL intelligence from query history and lineage. Acceldata shipped **Agentic Data Management**. Same industry-wide bet, arriving from opposite ends.
- **Both are enterprise, hybrid-deployment, audit-heavy.** Long sales cycles, on-prem requirements, and UIs that must show a full trail of who changed what.

## Why this matters for the frontend job

The overlap is not really in the domain. It is in the **shape of the interface problem**, and that argument is stronger than the domain one:

1. **Both render backend orchestration state a user did not author.** Your Governance Workflows UI rendered a DAG the engine executed and mutated. Their pipeline and agent UIs render runs and incidents. Same problem: represent a long-running, partially-complete, externally-mutated process without leaking the engine's primitives at the user.
2. **Both need schema-driven UI.** Automation Studio's nodes rendered their own config forms from a backend contract, so new node types shipped without frontend changes. An observability product with a growing catalog of checks, connectors and agents has exactly that pressure.
3. **Both are audit-first.** Governance Workflows had activity logs and a governance trail because an auditor asks *who approved this and when*. Acceldata's agents take autonomous actions against production data — the same question gets asked, harder.
4. **Both are approval and human-in-the-loop surfaces.** Anyone-approves / all-approve-parallel / all-approve-sequential is a human-in-the-loop routing problem. So is "the agent wants to remediate this — who signs off?"

## How to actually say it

If he offers you the easy version — *"it's basically the same space as Atlan, right?"* — take it, then sharpen it:

> "Adjacent, and the overlap is real, but they're not the same question. Atlan answers 'what is this data, who owns it, who's allowed to change it.' Acceldata answers 'is it correct, is it fresh, did the pipeline break, what's it costing.' Where they meet is data quality and lineage — and increasingly agents, since Atlan shipped Context Agents Studio around the same time you shipped Agentic Data Management.
>
> What actually transfers isn't the domain, though — it's the interface problem. Everything I built at Atlan was a UI over a long-running orchestration engine the user didn't author: a workflow DAG being executed and mutated by a backend, rendered so the user sees their approval, not the engine's state machine. Pipeline runs and agent actions are the same shape."

That answer does three things: it corrects him without contradicting him, it proves you researched both companies, and it moves the conversation onto ground where your experience is strongest.

## One honest gap to have an answer for

You have **not** worked in observability, monitoring or time-series UI. Atlan is state-and-approval; Acceldata is streams, metrics, alerts and charts at high cardinality. If he probes, do not paper over it:

> "I haven't built monitoring UI at that cardinality — that's the genuinely new part for me. What I have built is dense, state-heavy interfaces over async backends, plus the Automation Studio result inspector with tabular, JSON and CSV views over intermediate dataframes, which is the closest thing I've done to rendering a lot of data a user needs to scan quickly."

Naming the gap yourself, with the nearest real experience attached, is far stronger than being caught not having thought about it.

learnings.title: Governance Workflows — the project they will dig into hardest
learnings.source: docs.atlan.com governance workflow docs + your portfolio/resume
learnings.answer:
This is the headline item on your resume — *"Architected and bootstrapped the frontend for Governance Workflows, a no-code workflow automation platform; owned core modules enabling conditional routing and the request task inbox."* Expect the hiring manager to spend ten minutes here. Everything below is checked against Atlan's live public docs, so your vocabulary matches the product as it ships today.

## What the product actually is, in Atlan's own words

Governance Workflows lets an admin set controls on **data access management, metadata enrichment and new entity creation**, with out-of-the-box templates and automated execution. It lives at **Settings → Governance workflow**.

**Four templates ship:**

| Template | What it governs |
| --- | --- |
| Change Management | Metadata modifications — descriptions, certificates, aliases, term links, ownership, tags, custom metadata, domains, READMEs, announcements |
| New Entity Creation | Creation of glossaries, categories, terms, tags, data products, AI models/applications |
| Access Management | Access requests for tables, views, materialized views |
| Policy Approval | Requires the Policy Center module |

**The creation flow is three steps:** name/description/icon → **Define Scope** (asset filters using *Match all* = AND or *Match any* = OR) → **Set Routing & Approval**.

## The two modules you owned

### 1. Conditional routing

Only **Change Management** and **New Entity Creation** support conditional branching.

- Change Management branches trigger on *which attribute changed* — Name, Description, Certificate, Owners, Tags, Terms, custom metadata.
- New Entity Creation branches route on *destination* — glossary or category level — which lets each branch present a different input form.
- **Ceiling: 10 branches.**
- A **fallback path** catches anything no condition matched, and supports exclusions for specific attributes.

> The fallback path is the detail worth leading with. A router without a default is a router that silently drops requests — a request that matches nothing has to go *somewhere* or the requester waits forever on a workflow that never started. Framing it that way shows you were thinking about the failure mode, not just the happy path.

**Approval strategies — exact product names:**

| Name in the product | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| **Anyone approves** | One approver completes it |
| **All approve - Parallel** | Every approver must approve; order irrelevant |
| **All approve - Sequential** | Every approver must approve, in a defined order — approvers are drag-reorderable |

Your resume phrases these as *anyone-approves / all-approve-parallel / all-approve-sequential*. That is correct — use the product's spacing and capitalisation if you write it down.

**Auto-approval** is a *separate* toggle — **"Auto approve request"** — not a fourth strategy. It can be scoped by asset subset, by specific users/groups, or by asset owner. Atlan's own documented example is auto-approving access requests from new joiners to speed onboarding.

Two more mechanics worth having ready:

- **Asset-owner approval requires at least one additional approver.** An owner cannot be the sole approver of a change to their own asset.
- **Approval windows are set in days**; no action inside the window is an **automatic rejection**, and the requester is notified through the inbox.

### 2. The request task inbox

Requests and Governance Workflows are two systems that meet here:

- **Requests** is the general mechanism — *"Requests allow users to suggest changes to assets that they cannot directly change themselves."* Lifecycle is **Pending → Approved / Rejected**. The UX is deliberately invisible: the user edits the field as if they had permission, and Atlan converts the save into a request.
- **Once Governance Workflows + Inbox are enabled**, requests against *governed* assets stop being ad-hoc approvals and get routed through the configured workflow instead.

That sentence is the seam you built across. Know it cold.

**States differ by surface** — a real detail, and the kind of thing that reads as firsthand:

- Request lifecycle: **Pending / Approved / Rejected**
- Monitor tab filters: **Open / Approved / Rejected / Archived**
- Workflow definitions: **Published / Draft / Disabled**

Management is three tabs — **Overview** (activity by status/type, default 14-day window, adjustable to 7/30/45/custom), **Definitions** (filter by Published/Draft/Disabled), **Monitor** (filter requests, filter by requester, view the governance trail).

## The engineering constraint underneath it

Atlan's engineering blog published the orchestration engine design ([Janakiram G, Feb 2025](https://blog.atlan.com/engineering/building-a-scalable-engine-for-no-code-workflows/)). The single most useful fact for you:

> **The same spec JSON serves three purposes — UI rendering, execution traversal, and audit/debug.** The frontend renders directly off the document the engine executes and mutates. There is no separate frontend DTO.

The spec is a custom JSON DAG explicitly inspired by AWS Step Functions and Argo Workflows:

```json
{
  "dag": {
    "entrypoint": "first-block",
    "exitpoints": ["last-block-1", "last-block-2"],
    "tasks": [
      {
        "name": "Description of the block",
        "type": "NOTIFICATION",
        "arguments": [
          { "recipient": "example@email.com" },
          { "payload": { "title": "...", "description": "..." } }
        ],
        "depends": "auto-approval-block.SUCCESS || manual-approval-block.SUCCESS",
        "status": "PENDING",
        "updated_at": "<unix-timestamp>"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Three things fall out of that shape, and each is a good answer to "what was hard":

1. **`depends` is an Argo-style boolean expression** over other task ids and their terminal states. Your conditional-routing UI had to author and validate that expression — which means the builder is not really a form, it is an expression editor with a graph behind it.
2. **`status` lives per task, not per workflow.** So the UI must render *partial* completion — some tasks done, some pending, some blocked on a dependency that has not resolved. A single workflow-level status bar would have been a lie.
3. **State propagation is CDC-driven, not polled** — the engine "reacts to state changes in the store" (Apache Atlas, CDC-enabled). The blog does **not** state the browser transport, so describe your own implementation from memory rather than attributing it to the post.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  req[User edits a governed asset] --> intercept[Save intercepted → Request created]
  intercept --> scope{Scope filter\nMatch all / Match any}
  scope -->|no match| direct[Ad-hoc approval path]
  scope -->|match| wf[Governance Workflow triggered]
  wf --> branch{Conditional branch\nmax 10}
  branch -->|attribute matched| b1[Branch: routing + approvers]
  branch -->|nothing matched| fb[Fallback path]
  b1 --> auto{Auto approve request?}
  fb --> auto
  auto -->|yes| done[Approved]
  auto -->|no| strat[Anyone approves /\nAll approve - Parallel /\nAll approve - Sequential]
  strat --> inbox[Task inbox]
  inbox --> done
  inbox --> rej[Rejected or expired]
```

## The edge case that makes you sound senior

Governance workflows are **explicitly not triggered** by:

- spreadsheet-tool bulk updates
- Playbook bulk updates
- Atlan AI bulk operations
- API / SDK / CLI bulk operations
- browser-extension metadata edits

This is a genuinely interesting governance hole — the controls apply to the UI path and not the programmatic ones. If the conversation goes anywhere near "how do you think about gaps in a system you built," this is your answer. It also sets up a good opinion: *the right fix is enforcing at the metadata-store write path rather than at each client, but that is a much larger change and it was not mine to make.*

## Questions to expect, and answers

**"Why did you need a centralised orchestration layer at all — why not let each widget own its logic?"**
Because the spec is shared with the engine. Every widget that hand-rolled its own reading of the task JSON became a place the backend contract could break. Centralising it meant one adapter between the DAG document and the widget tree. See the dedicated entry on that migration.

**"How did you validate a workflow before publishing?"**
Talk through: unreachable tasks (nothing depends on them and they are not the entrypoint), cycles in the DAG, branches with no approver, a missing fallback, and an approval window of zero. Be honest about which of these you actually shipped versus which you would add.

**"Ten branches is a low ceiling. Why?"**
A good answer says the ceiling is a product decision, not a technical one — past about ten branches the routing table stops being readable in a visual builder and the customer actually wants a rules table or several narrower workflows. A branch is a fork a human has to reason about during an audit.

**"What happens if the workflow definition changes while a request is in flight?"**
Know your answer. The honest one is that the in-flight request executes against the spec document it started with, because the document *is* the execution state. Changing the definition creates a new version for subsequent requests.

**"Sequential approval — what if approver two is on leave?"**
Approval windows are in days and expiry auto-rejects. Discuss delegation, reminders, and whether auto-rejection is the right default for a blocked approver versus escalation.

**"How did you test this?"**
Your resume claims unit testing, analytics instrumentation and feature flags as platform foundations for Automation Studio. For Governance Workflows, be specific about what you actually had — RTL for the builder, fixtures for the spec JSON, and whatever integration coverage existed. Do not inflate this; "we had less than I wanted, here's what I'd add" is a strong senior answer.

## What to say you'd do differently

Pick one and mean it. Candidates:

- The bulk-operation gap above — enforcement belongs at the write path.
- Versioning of workflow definitions, if that was thin.
- A simulator: given this asset and this change, show me which branch fires and who approves. Governance UIs are hard to trust without one.

> ⚠️ Verify before the interview: how many branches you actually shipped versus the documented 10; whether the fallback path existed from day one or came later; and whether the approval-expiry behaviour was yours or backend-owned.

learnings.title: The orchestration layer — defending "days per widget → hours"
learnings.source: Your resume bullet + blog.atlan.com engineering posts
learnings.answer:
Your resume says: *"Implemented a centralized orchestration layer decoupling workflow logic from individual UI widgets, reducing attribute migration from days per widget to hours."*

That is the only hard efficiency number on your Atlan experience. A hiring manager who is any good will pick at it, because unsubstantiated ratios are the most common resume inflation there is. This entry exists so the number survives contact.

## Why the number is attackable

Three obvious challenges:

1. **"Days to hours" is a ~10× claim. Measured how?**
2. **"Attribute migration" — what is that, exactly?** It is internal jargon; he has no idea what it means.
3. **How many widgets?** A 10× saving on two widgets is a weekend. On forty it is a quarter.

Answer the second one *first*, unprompted. The claim is unintelligible until he knows what the unit of work was.

## The setup — what made it slow

From Atlan's published engine design, the workflow spec is a JSON DAG where each task carries `type`, `arguments`, `depends`, `status`, `updated_at` — and critically, **the same spec document drives UI rendering, execution traversal and audit** ([Atlan engineering, Feb 2025](https://blog.atlan.com/engineering/building-a-scalable-engine-for-no-code-workflows/)).

That design is elegant on the backend and unforgiving on the frontend: every widget that reads the spec directly is coupled to the engine's document shape. So when an attribute moved, was renamed, gained a nested shape, or when a new task `type` shipped, every widget that touched it had to be found and changed by hand.

The backend could add task types cheaply — dispatch is reflection-based, new `type` means a new registered Go function and the pipeline infra stays frozen. **The asymmetry is the story.** The backend could ship a new node type in an afternoon; the frontend needed a widget-by-widget sweep to catch up. Your layer removed that asymmetry.

```
Before                             After
──────                             ─────
spec JSON                          spec JSON
   │                                  │
   ├──► widget A (own parsing)        └──► orchestration layer
   ├──► widget B (own parsing)               │  (one adapter: spec ⇄ widget model)
   ├──► widget C (own parsing)               ├──► widget A (props only)
   └──► widget D (own parsing)               ├──► widget B (props only)
                                             ├──► widget C (props only)
   n places to change per attribute          └──► widget D (props only)
                                             1 place to change per attribute
```

## How to state the metric so it holds

Do not lead with "10×." Lead with the mechanism, and let the number land as the consequence:

> "Every widget parsed the workflow spec itself, so an attribute change meant finding and editing each one, then re-testing each one. I put one adapter between the spec document and the widget tree — widgets take props now, they don't read the document. After that a migration is an edit in one place plus a regression pass, so the same change went from a multi-day sweep to an afternoon."

Then, if he presses on measurement, be honest about what kind of number it is:

> "It's an engineering-time estimate from the tickets, not an instrumented metric — I'm comparing migrations we did before the layer against ones after."

**Say that.** Claiming precision you don't have is the actual risk here; a candidate who volunteers the limits of their own number is far more credible than one who defends it as though it came off a dashboard.

## The questions behind the question

He is not really auditing arithmetic. He is checking three things:

| He asks | He is testing |
| --- | --- |
| "How did you measure it?" | Do you distinguish an estimate from a measurement? |
| "Why hadn't anyone done it already?" | Can you describe org reality without blaming people? |
| "What did it cost?" | Do you know refactors have a price? |

For the second: this is the honest shape of it — the per-widget pattern was fine at three widgets, and nobody re-litigates a working pattern while shipping features. It stops being fine somewhere around the tenth. Recognising the crossover point *is* the contribution.

For the third, have real costs ready: the migration period where both patterns coexisted, the indirection cost when someone debugging now has to step through an adapter, and the risk that the abstraction is wrong for a future node type. If you found a case the layer handled badly, lead with it.

## This is also your "made a call others disagreed with" story

If he asks for conflict or for a decision you had to defend — and in a techno-managerial round he will — this is the strongest one you have, because it has a real trade-off on both sides. Centralising costs you flexibility per widget and buys you consistency. Someone reasonably preferred the flexibility. Describe their argument fairly before you describe why you went the other way; interviewers weight that heavily.

## Related

- The product this sat under: [Governance Workflows](/acceldata-prep/4)
- The canvas that inherited the pattern: [Automation Studio](/acceldata-prep/6)

> ⚠️ Verify before the interview: roughly how many widgets there were; whether the layer landed before or after Automation Studio started; and one concrete attribute migration you can name and walk through end to end. One specific example beats the ratio entirely.

learnings.title: Automation Studio — schema-driven nodes and live execution
learnings.answer:
Your resume: *"Shipped core capabilities for Automation Studio, a no-code/low-code workflow orchestration platform, including schema-driven node configuration, real-time execution visualization, and node-level result inspection; established platform foundations with unit testing, analytics instrumentation, and feature flags."*

This is your most recent Atlan work (2025–2026) and the closest in shape to what Acceldata's agent and pipeline UIs have to do. Lead with it if he asks what you are proudest of.

## The three capabilities, and why each is hard

### 1. Schema-driven node configuration

**The claim:** every node renders its own config form from a backend contract, so new node types ship without frontend changes.

**Why it matters, stated in one line:** the backend could already add task types cheaply — dispatch is reflection-based, so a new task `type` is a new registered function and the pipeline infrastructure stays frozen ([Atlan engineering](https://blog.atlan.com/engineering/building-a-scalable-engine-for-no-code-workflows/)). If the frontend needed a code change and a release for every new node, the frontend became the bottleneck on the backend's flexibility. Schema-driven config removes the frontend from that path entirely.

**Be ready for the obvious follow-ups.** These are where the real conversation is:

- *"What happens when the schema can't express what a node needs?"* Every schema-driven system has an escape hatch. Know yours — a custom-component registry keyed by node type, a `x-ui` hint block in the schema, or an accepted list of special cases. If you had no escape hatch, say so and say what broke.
- *"How do you validate?"* Schema-level validation (types, required, ranges) versus cross-field rules versus rules only the backend can check. Where did each live?
- *"How do you version it?"* A workflow saved against schema v1 opened after the backend ships v2. This is the genuinely hard one. Migrate on read, store the version alongside the config, or refuse to open? Have a position.
- *"What about a bad schema in production?"* Does one malformed node type take down the canvas, or degrade to a raw JSON editor for that node? Graceful degradation is the senior answer.

> Worth knowing: Atlan later moved UI config from **Kubernetes ConfigMaps to an app-served `/uiconfigs` endpoint** during the Temporal migration. If your schemas came from ConfigMaps, that transition is a good thing to reference.

### 2. Real-time execution visualisation

Per-node status, timing and failure surfacing as the run streams in.

The engine's model constrains this, and knowing the constraint is the point:

- **Status is per task**, carried on the task node in the spec document alongside `updated_at`. There is no single workflow status to bind to — so the canvas has to render **partial completion**: some nodes done, some running, some pending, some blocked on a `depends` expression that has not resolved.
- **Propagation is CDC-driven, not polled** — the engine "reacts to state changes in the store" rather than being polled.
- **`depends` is an Argo-style boolean expression** (`"a.SUCCESS || b.SUCCESS"`). So "blocked" is not one state — a node can be waiting on a dependency that may still succeed, or permanently unreachable because its expression can no longer be satisfied. Those look identical if you only model pending/running/done, and they are completely different to a user staring at a stuck run.

That last distinction is the kind of detail that wins a technical conversation. If you modelled it, say so. If you did not, it is an excellent "what I'd do differently."

> ⚠️ The engineering blog never states the browser transport — WebSocket, SSE or GraphQL subscription. Describe what you actually built from memory; do not attribute a mechanism to the blog.

Expect: *"What if the user has the canvas open for an hour?"* — reconnection, backfill after a dropped connection, and whether you re-fetch full state or replay a delta. And: *"A run with 200 nodes streaming updates — what breaks?"* Re-render storms, layout thrash, and whether you batched updates per frame.

### 3. Node-level result inspection

Tabular, JSON and CSV views over intermediate dataframes.

This is your **closest existing experience to an observability product**, so give it more airtime than its one resume line suggests. Talking points: virtualisation for large result sets, type inference for column rendering, how much you fetched versus streamed, truncation and its honesty (does the user know they are seeing the first 1,000 rows?), and CSV export mechanics.

Atlan's own platform-transformation post is useful context here: it criticises the older architecture for lacking **"introspectable execution state"** — no breakpoints, no replay, debugging as *"archaeological digs through logs."* Result inspection is the frontend's answer to exactly that complaint. Framing your feature as the fix for a documented platform gap is much stronger than describing it as a viewer.

### 4. Platform foundations

Unit testing, analytics instrumentation, feature flags. Short but load-bearing — it is the difference between "shipped a feature" and "set up how features ship here."

Be concrete: which test library, what coverage actually looked like, what the analytics answered (which node types get used? where do people abandon a build?), and how flags were scoped — per tenant, per user, per environment. Acceldata's hybrid/on-prem model makes flag scoping a genuinely interesting problem, and the JD's "shared front-end components across all products" says they have the same pressure.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  be[Backend node registry] -->|schema| cfg[Node config form]
  cfg --> canvas[Canvas]
  canvas -->|spec JSON| engine[Orchestration engine]
  engine -->|CDC state changes| status[Per-node status + timing]
  status --> canvas
  engine --> results[(Intermediate dataframes)]
  results --> inspect[Result inspector\ntable / JSON / CSV]
```

## The line that connects this to Acceldata

> "Automation Studio was a canvas where the user composes a pipeline, ships it, and then watches it run — nodes that configure themselves from a backend schema, live per-node status as the run streams, and the ability to click any node and see what it actually produced. That's structurally the same job as showing someone what an autonomous agent did to their data and letting them inspect it."

## Related

- The layer this inherited: [The orchestration layer](/acceldata-prep/5)
- The agent equivalent you're building now: [The verification agent](/acceldata-prep/9)

> ⚠️ Verify: which parts were yours versus the team's; whether schema-driven config was your design or inherited; and the real transport for live updates.

learnings.title: Visual Form Builder — the reusable-primitive argument
learnings.answer:
Your resume: *"Designed a visual form builder for composing custom forms via drag-and-drop field ordering, validation, and configurable input fields; adopted across governance workflow modules and data products."*

The word doing the work is **adopted**. Anyone can build a form builder. Building one that other teams chose to consume rather than fork is a platform outcome, and that is the framing to lead with.

## What shipped, per the live docs

**Exactly six field types:**

| Type | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Text | Free-form |
| Dropdown | Predefined values |
| Email | Text with email-format validation |
| Number | Numeric |
| Date | UTC |
| **Custom metadata property** | Surfaces an existing custom metadata property as a form field |

That last one is the interesting one — it is the seam between the form builder and the custom metadata system. A form field is not always a new piece of data; sometimes it is a window onto a property the org already modelled. That coupling is worth mentioning because it shows the builder was designed into the platform, not bolted beside it.

**Field configuration:** name and description required; optional placeholder ("add instructions to help users complete the field"); a **Required** toggle that blocks submission; fields reorderable, deletable and **duplicable**.

**Lifecycle:** **Published / Draft / Disabled**, with *Save as draft*, *Preview*, and transitions from Draft or Published into Disabled.

**Consumption:** forms embed only in **Access Management** and **New Entity Creation** workflow templates, via the **"Require requestor information"** toggle, which links an existing form or creates a new one. The purpose, in Atlan's words, is to *"collect more information from requesters as they raise requests, thus enabling approvers to make informed decisions."*

**Two documented limitations, both worth raising yourself:**

- **Forms cannot be deleted — only disabled.**
- **Markdown is not supported** in descriptions or fields.

## The no-delete decision is your best talking point here

If you volunteer one design decision from this project, make it this one. It looks like a missing feature and it is actually a correctness requirement:

> "Forms can be disabled but never deleted. That's deliberate — a form's submitted responses are attached to historical requests, and those requests are part of a governance audit trail. Deleting the form orphans the answers, so an auditor looking at an approval from eight months ago can't see what question was actually asked. Disable keeps the record intact and stops new use. It looks like a gap until you think about who reads the audit log."

That single answer demonstrates you understood the product domain, not just the component. In a governance product, **immutability of the audit trail beats tidiness of the admin UI** — and that instinct transfers directly to a company whose agents take autonomous actions and have to prove what they did.

## Questions to expect

**"Why only six field types?"**
Each type is a contract with three consumers — the builder UI, the request-submission renderer, and the approver's read view. Six types that work everywhere beats twenty that work in one place. Also note the field types map onto what the platform can actually *do* with an answer; a rich-text blob no workflow can route on is a field that looks useful and isn't.

**"How is the schema serialised?"**
Your resume says "serialised to a portable schema." Be ready to sketch it: ordered field list, per-field type, label, description, placeholder, required flag, type-specific config (dropdown options, custom-metadata property reference). Discuss whether order was an array position or an explicit index, and what happens to existing responses when a published form is edited.

**"Drag-and-drop — what did you use, and what was hard?"**
The interesting part is not the library. It is keyboard accessibility (a drag-only reorder is unusable for some people — did you ship an alternative?), touch, and the announcement of position changes to a screen reader. Your GSoC work was explicitly accessibility-heavy, so this connects.

**"Published form gets edited — what happens to in-flight requests?"**
Same class of problem as changing a workflow definition mid-flight. Have a consistent answer across both.

**"How did you get other teams to adopt it instead of forking?"**
This is the real question if he is a hiring manager rather than an architect. The honest mechanics: it had to cover their cases, be documented, be stable, and be less work than forking. Adoption across governance workflows *and* data products means at least one team chose it who did not have to.

## What to say you'd do differently

- Markdown in field descriptions is a real gap — governance forms ask complicated questions and plain text limits how well you can explain them. Know why it was excluded (sanitisation? consistent rendering across the three consumers?).
- Conditional fields — show field B only if field A is X. Almost every form builder eventually needs it; it is also where they become unmaintainable. A view on where that line sits is a good answer.

## Related

- The workflows that consume these forms: [Governance Workflows](/acceldata-prep/4)
- The custom metadata a form field can point at: [Custom Metadata & Integrations](/acceldata-prep/8)

> ⚠️ Verify: whether all six field types were yours or some came later; whether the custom-metadata field type was your design; and which teams actually adopted it — one named non-obvious consumer is worth more than the word "adopted."

learnings.title: Custom Metadata & Integrations — extensibility and four auth models
learnings.answer:
Two resume bullets, one theme: **letting customers change the system without a release.** Your longest-running Atlan work (2021–2025) and the least glamorous — which makes it the one you should be able to talk about most concretely.

## Custom metadata

Atlan ships basic metadata — certification, owners, descriptions. Custom metadata lets an organisation extend that with its own properties, relationships and validation rules, **without waiting for Atlan to ship a release**.

**Structure:** properties are organised into **metadata groups** — user-defined categories. Atlan's own documented examples are an "IPR" group for intellectual-property fields and an "ETL" group for processing-engine details.

**Value restrictions confirmed in the docs:** date values, boolean values, and predefined options (enumerated dropdowns).

> ⚠️ The full property-type list is not stated on the public concept page. Your resume claims "typed properties spanning options, users, groups, SQL and rich text" — that is firsthand knowledge and almost certainly right, but the docs do not corroborate it, so state it as your own recollection rather than as documented fact.

**One mechanic worth knowing:** a property needs **"Show in filter"** enabled before it appears as a filter option inside Playbooks. That is a small toggle with a large implication — every custom property is a potential facet, and turning them all on would make the filter UI unusable. Someone had to decide that surfacing is opt-in. If that was you, say so.

**The question he will ask:** *"Customers define arbitrary typed properties — how does the UI stay coherent?"* This is the heart of it. Talk about: rendering a property you have never seen before, the type → widget mapping, what happens when a type is removed or changed after values exist (Atlan has a documented FAQ on exactly this — "Can I update input type for existing custom metadata"), and how you keep a table readable when a customer has defined sixty properties.

**Elasticsearch is worth mentioning.** Your portfolio lists it in this project's stack, and Acceldata's own Bangalore JD lists Elasticsearch under expected data-layer exposure. Arbitrary user-defined properties that must remain searchable and filterable is a real indexing problem — dynamic mappings, field explosion, and how you query across properties whose names you did not know at build time.

## Integrations — Slack, Jira, ServiceNow, Microsoft Teams

Your resume says *"one configuration flow across integrations with very different auth and capability models."* The docs show just how different, and this is the substance of the story:

| Integration | Auth model | The awkward part |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Slack** | **Token-based, not OAuth scopes** — access + refresh token generated in Slack's app console, then a workspace install | Tokens **expire in ~12 hours**, so they must be used the same day they are generated. Also: **channels must be public** for Atlan to post |
| **Jira Cloud** | **True OAuth 2.0** — `read:jira-user`, `read:jira-work`, `write:jira-work`, `manage:jira-configuration`, `offline_access` | Separate integration path for **Jira Data Center**. Per-project allowed issue types, plus a default project |
| **ServiceNow** | OAuth 2.0 with a dedicated **`atlan.service`** account and `atlan_service_account_role`; callback at `https://<instance>/oauth-callback` | Requires importing an **Update Set XML** into ServiceNow, which installs an **"Atlan Business Rule"** for bidirectional sync. **Requires governance workflows + inbox already enabled** |
| **Microsoft Teams** | Two app versions — **native marketplace v3** (recommended, Microsoft-verified) and **legacy custom app v2** (deprecated, needs the customer's Azure AD admin) | Supporting a deprecated and a current path simultaneously |

### The story to tell

> "Four integrations, four genuinely different auth models — one is short-lived tokens pasted from a developer console, one is standard OAuth scopes, one needs a service account plus an update set imported into the customer's own ServiceNow instance, and one has a deprecated and a current app version live at the same time. The product requirement was that they all look like one thing: go to Integrations, click Connect, configure, done.
>
> So the surface is one flow with a per-integration strategy underneath — each one declares what credentials it needs, what its connect step looks like, and what configuration it exposes once connected. The alternative is four bespoke pages that drift, and that's what happens by default when integrations get added one at a time by whoever needs them."

**Then volunteer the hardest part**, because it is the best detail here: the **Slack 12-hour token expiry**. A credential that dies overnight means the setup flow has a *time limit* — a user who starts configuring, gets pulled into a meeting and comes back tomorrow has a broken connection with no obvious cause. What does the UI do? Explain the deadline up front, detect the expired state and say so specifically rather than showing a generic failure, and make re-auth one click rather than a re-read of the docs. Error states are where integration UIs are actually judged.

**ServiceNow is your depth card.** It needs the customer's ServiceNow admin to create an OAuth endpoint, provision a service account, and import an XML update set — that is a multi-person, multi-system setup, and the frontend's job is to make a sequence like that legible and resumable. It is also the one that **requires governance workflows and inbox to be enabled first**, which ties this project directly to [Governance Workflows](/acceldata-prep/4).

## Why this matters at Acceldata

Acceldata is hybrid, on-prem and sovereign by design, sells into banks and life sciences, and their ServiceNow Data Catalog partnership means they are solving the same class of problem. **An integrations surface across many third-party systems with mismatched auth is a permanent feature of enterprise data tooling.** You have done it four times. That is directly, boringly relevant — which is exactly the kind of relevance hiring managers like.

## Related

- The workflows ServiceNow plugs into: [Governance Workflows](/acceldata-prep/4)
- Custom metadata as a form field type: [Visual Form Builder](/acceldata-prep/7)

> ⚠️ Verify: whether you built all four or inherited some; whether the "one configuration flow" was your design or predated you; and the exact custom metadata property types, since the docs don't list them.

learnings.title: The verification agent — your highest-leverage story
learnings.source: Your portfolio + resume; Acceldata agentic positioning
learnings.answer:
**Spend the most preparation time here.** Acceldata relaunched four months ago as an "Autonomous Data & AI Platform" selling agents that detect, diagnose and autonomously remediate problems in production data. You are currently building an agent system whose entire design thesis is *constrain what the model is allowed to decide*. That is not adjacent — that is the same argument.

## What you built, from your resume

> *"Shipped a data-entry agent that checks a candidate's submission before verification runs: a declared state machine driven by NATS events, deterministic Go pre-fetch of candidate, package and profile, and the model confined to a single judgement step."*
>
> *"Authored a 17-tool bank behind the agent — OCR-to-form comparison across 15 document types, cross-check and cross-document matching, pincode reference lookups, timeline and employment-gap analysis, payslip arithmetic, and free-text plausibility — keeping every rule-based decision in Go so the model only judges what no rule can decide."*
>
> *"Defined the agent's structured output contract (verdict, confidence, per-field severity) and built the Next.js reviewer console it drives: one row per answer grouped by check, colour-coded from the agent's judgements, with accept / correct / raise-to-candidate actions."*

Stack: Next.js, React, Golang, Eino, Amazon Bedrock, Langfuse, Temporal, NATS, GraphQL, Redis.

## The thesis, in one paragraph

Say this early and say it confidently, because it is a genuine engineering opinion and most candidates do not have one:

> "The design rule is that the model doesn't get to decide anything a rule can decide. Pincode lookups, date arithmetic, employment-gap calculation, payslip maths, cross-document field matching — all of that is deterministic Go, because it's checkable, testable and identical every run. The model gets exactly one job: judge the things no rule can, like whether a free-text explanation is plausible. That's why there are 17 tools and one judgement step, not one big prompt. It makes the agent auditable — for any verdict you can point at which rule fired and which part the model actually decided."

Three reasons this lands:

1. It is an **opinion with a cost**, not a list of technologies. More engineering in Go, less flexibility than a general agent.
2. It is exactly the problem an autonomous data platform has. An agent that remediates a pipeline must be able to show which part was deterministic and which was inference — and Acceldata's own materials emphasise **audit trails** over agent actions.
3. It directly answers "how do you make an agent trustworthy," which is *the* question in that product category right now.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  ev[NATS event] --> sm[Declared state machine]
  sm --> pre[Deterministic Go pre-fetch\ncandidate · package · profile]
  pre --> tools[17-tool bank\nOCR compare · cross-doc match · pincode\ntimeline gaps · payslip arithmetic]
  tools --> rules{Can a rule decide it?}
  rules -->|yes| det[Deterministic verdict]
  rules -->|no| model[Model — single judgement step]
  det --> out[Structured output\nverdict · confidence · per-field severity]
  model --> out
  out --> console[Reviewer console]
  console --> acc[Accept]
  console --> cor[Correct]
  console --> esc[Raise to candidate]
```

## The frontend half — do not let this get lost

You are interviewing for a **frontend** role. The agent architecture is the hook; the reviewer console is the job.

The output contract — **verdict, confidence, per-field severity** — is what makes the UI possible, and the fact that *you defined the contract and then built its consumer* is the strongest thing here. It is the same instinct as Automation Studio's schema-driven nodes: get the contract right and the interface follows.

Have real answers on:

- **Why one row per answer, grouped by check?** Because a reviewer works field by field, not document by document — they are asking "is this answer right," not "is this PDF good."
- **How is confidence rendered?** This is the hard one and a great thing to have thought about. A number is meaningless to a reviewer; what they need is a decision — look at this, or don't. Do you threshold it into bands, sort by it, or use it only to order the queue? Any considered answer beats "we showed the percentage."
- **Per-field severity → colour.** Then immediately: what about reviewers who cannot distinguish those colours? Your GSoC work included first-class colour-blind support. Saying "colour is never the only signal" here connects your oldest project to your newest and shows a consistent standard.
- **Accept / correct / raise-to-candidate.** Three actions with different weights — one confirms, one overrides the agent, one goes back to a human outside the company. What does the UI do to make the irreversible one feel different from the cheap one?
- **What happens when the agent is wrong?** Every override is training signal. Is it captured? Does the reviewer say *why* they overrode? Langfuse is in your stack — tie it in if that is what it was for.

## Questions to expect

**"Why a declared state machine rather than letting the agent plan?"**
Because a declared machine is inspectable before it runs and reproducible after. An agent that plans its own steps gives a different trace every time, which is unauditable in a compliance context — and background verification is a compliance context.

**"Why pre-fetch deterministically in Go instead of giving the model tools to fetch?"**
Latency, cost, and determinism. The data needed is known ahead of time, so fetching it is not a decision. Letting the model choose whether to fetch a record it always needs adds a round trip and a failure mode for nothing.

**"Seventeen tools is a lot. How do you keep the model from picking the wrong one?"**
The honest answer is that mostly it does not choose — the state machine sequences the deterministic work, and the model's surface is narrow by construction. Say that plainly; it is the point of the design.

**"How do you evaluate it?"**
Langfuse is in your stack, so know what you actually track — traces, latency, cost, and whether you have a labelled set with regression runs. If evaluation is thinner than you would like, say so and say what you would build. "We have tracing but not yet a proper eval harness, and here is what I'd want" is a credible senior answer; claiming a mature eval setup that does not exist is a trap.

**"How do you stop the model hallucinating a verdict?"**
Structured output with a fixed schema, the confinement to a single judgement step, and the fact that most fields never reach the model at all.

## The bridge to Acceldata

If he asks why this job — this is the sentence:

> "You've just launched a platform where agents take autonomous actions against production data, and the thing that makes or breaks that is whether a data engineer trusts what the agent did. I've spent the last few months building exactly that — an agent designed so every decision is attributable to either a rule or a single bounded judgement, and a reviewer console where a human can see, accept, correct or escalate each one. That's the interface problem I want to keep working on, and it's on top of five years of building UI over long-running backend orchestration."

## Related

- Where the interface instinct came from: [Automation Studio](/acceldata-prep/6)
- Why Acceldata specifically: [Why Acceldata, growth expectations, and what to ask him](/acceldata-prep/14)

> ⚠️ Verify: the split between what you built and what the team built; whether the 17 tools are all shipped; and what Langfuse is actually instrumented for. Do not overstate the eval maturity.

learnings.title: CircuitVerse / GSoC — the character card
learnings.answer:
Short entry, because it should be a short answer. This is not a technical depth story — it is a **character and trajectory** story, and it is stronger than you probably give it credit for.

## The facts

- **Google Summer of Code, CircuitVerse, 2020–2022** — Student Developer, then mentor across two seasons.
- Led design and implementation of the open-source simulator UI in **vanilla JavaScript and SCSS**.
- **Increased effective canvas workspace area by 19%.**
- Built a multi-theme engine with **six palettes** — Default, Night Sky, Lite-born Spring, G&W, High Contrast — plus custom theme authoring.
- First-class **accessibility and colour-blind support**: distinct wire states and component contrast for different vision needs.
- Modular dockable panels for timing diagrams, testbenches, element hierarchies and layout editing.
- [Wiki](https://github.com/CircuitVerse/CircuitVerse/wiki/GSoC%2720-Project-List#project-4---enhancing-simulator-user-interface) · [Final report](https://blog.circuitverse.org/posts/project_4_final_report/)

## What it demonstrates

**Real users, no framework.** A simulator canvas in vanilla JS and SCSS, used by students and educators worldwide. It shows you can reason about layout, rendering and state without React holding the structure for you — and it is the only thing on your resume that proves that.

**19% is a measured number.** Unlike the days-to-hours claim, this one has a public final report behind it. If he asks how you measured it, you can point at the report — and the mechanism is easy to explain: the redesign moved chrome out of the canvas's way, so the usable drawing area grew.

**Accessibility as a default, not a retrofit.** Colour-blind support with distinct wire states is a real design constraint, not an audit checkbox. It matters more than it looks in an interview for an **observability product**, where status is conveyed by colour constantly — red pipeline, amber warning, green healthy. Someone who has already built a UI where colour is never the sole signal is someone who will not ship an unreadable alert dashboard.

**Six themes plus custom authoring** is a design-token problem solved in 2020 without a design-token library. That is the origin of the design-systems thread that runs through your Atlan work.

**Mentoring, twice.** You did the project, then came back to mentor others across two seasons. In a **hiring manager** round this is worth real weight — it is evidence of the thing managers are actually assessing when they ask about growth and ownership, and it predates any job title.

## How to tell it — 30 seconds, not three minutes

> "I did GSoC with CircuitVerse — an open-source digital logic simulator used by students. I led the simulator UI redesign in vanilla JS and SCSS, got about 19% more usable canvas area by restructuring the chrome, and built a theme engine with six palettes plus custom themes, including proper colour-blind support so wire states stay distinguishable. Then I came back and mentored contributors for two more seasons. It's the reason I care about accessibility and design tokens by default rather than as a cleanup pass."

Then stop. If he is interested he will ask. Spending five minutes on a 2020 student project when you have shipped platform features at a data governance company is a misallocation.

## When to deploy it

- **"Tell me about yourself"** — one clause, as the origin of the design-systems and accessibility thread.
- **"Have you mentored anyone?"** — this is the answer, and it is earlier and more voluntary than most candidates can offer.
- **"Any open source?"** — this is the answer. It is also the only public code of yours he can go and read.
- **"Why frontend?"** — a genuine one. You chose it, in public, unpaid, before anyone was paying you for it.

## Related

- Where the accessibility standard shows up again: [The verification agent](/acceldata-prep/9)
- Ownership stories: [Six ownership stories, mapped to the questions they answer](/acceldata-prep/12)

learnings.title: The HM round — what he is actually scoring
learnings.source: Recruiter call transcript, 2026-09 + Glassdoor process reports
learnings.answer:
Read this first on the day. Everything the recruiter told you about this round, decoded.

## What he said, verbatim

> "In the hiring manager round it is often a techno-managerial round… he might ask you to design also or he might ask you some of the technical questions… and in terms of the projects, in terms of your aspiration to join Acceldata… because you're outside Bangalore, he might ask you how desperate are you to come to Bangalore, because it shouldn't waste anybody's time, including yours and his."

> "The end-to-end ownership that you have taken, how much curiosity you show for the learning purpose, and what sort of growth you are expecting… **at least 60 to 70% will be technical, the rest managerial.**"

> "Go through Acceldata — what we do, our products, a little bit of knowledge about the products and about the investors."

> "Be confident and answer all the questions, prepare for it. That's all — the other things I'll take care of."

## The scoring rubric, decoded

| What he asks about | What he is actually measuring |
| --- | --- |
| Your projects (60–70% of the round) | Did you *build* this or were you *near* it? Depth is the tell |
| End-to-end ownership | Did you own outcomes, or complete tickets? |
| Curiosity / learning | Will you still be useful in two years, in a product that rebrands every 18 months? |
| Growth expectations | Can he actually offer what you want? A mismatch here kills offers late |
| Why Acceldata | Did you research, or are you interviewing everywhere? |
| Bangalore | Is this offer going to fall over at the last step? |

Note the order and the weight. **This is not a behavioural round with some tech in it.** It is a technical round run by a manager, plus four managerial questions he needs answered before he spends more of the team's time. Prepare for it like a technical round.

## The structure to expect

Glassdoor reports on Acceldata describe the process as HM discussion → two DSA rounds → system design → HR, though other candidates report a different order with the design round covering past projects. Your recruiter confirmed **HM first, then HLD**. Average reported process length is around 19 days; difficulty rated ~2.8/5.

So: this round gates the rest, and the depth questions land here rather than in the design round.

## The five things to get right

**1. Depth beats breadth.** He will pick one project and go three questions deep. The pattern is always: what did you build → why that way → what went wrong. Prepare to go *four* levels on [Governance Workflows](/acceldata-prep/4) and [the verification agent](/acceldata-prep/9). Being unable to answer the fourth question on your headline project is the single most common way this round is failed.

**2. Say "I" and "we" accurately.** Overclaiming is the fastest way to lose a manager, and it is trivially detectable — he just asks one more question. "I owned the routing and the inbox; the orchestration engine was the backend team; I designed the contract between them" is a *stronger* answer than claiming the whole thing, because it shows you know where your boundaries were.

**3. Have your own opinions, with costs attached.** "Every rule-based decision stays in Go so the model only judges what no rule can decide" is an opinion. So is "the fallback path is the important part of a router." So is "a form you can't delete is correct, because the audit trail outlives the form." Managers hire people who have views, not people who have résumés.

**4. Volunteer what went wrong.** For each major project have one real thing — a gap, a wrong call, a piece of debt. The bulk-operation gap in [governance workflows](/acceldata-prep/4) is perfect: a genuine hole in a system you built, that you can explain and have a view on fixing. Volunteering it makes everything else you say more credible.

**5. Land the agentic connection.** Do not wait to be asked. They relaunched four months ago around autonomous agents; you are building an agent whose entire design is about making it auditable. Get this into the conversation in the first ten minutes.

## Two traps specific to you

**The "why are you leaving after four months?" trap.** You joined AICraft Labs in April 2026 on a contract, after five years at Atlan. He will ask. The answer is short, factual, non-defensive, and does not criticise anyone:

> "It's a contract role — I went in to build the agent platform, and that's what I've been doing. I'm looking for the next long-term thing now, and after five years of building one product deeply I know that's the kind of work I want. Short tenure on a contract isn't the pattern of my career — the five years before it are."

Do not over-explain. One answer, then move on.

**The "you're a frontend engineer, why all the Go?" question.** Real and answerable: you are a frontend engineer who went and learned the backend his interfaces sit on. At an infrastructure company that is an asset, not a confusion. Be clear that frontend platform work is the role you want — this is the job you are interviewing for, and ambiguity here costs you.

## The 30 seconds before you speak

He said your voice broke up on the call. Use a wired headset, and if you are on mobile data, be somewhere with signal. He also said he would speak to the hiring manager for you — so you are going in with a recruiter who is already on your side.

learnings.title: Six ownership stories, mapped to the questions they answer
learnings.source: Built from your portfolio and resume — nothing invented
learnings.answer:
The recruiter named **end-to-end ownership** as a scored dimension. Managers ask for it through a small set of standard questions. Below are six stories drawn only from your actual experience, each tagged with the questions it answers.

Every one is in **Situation → Task → Action → Result** shape, but do not narrate the labels out loud. Just make sure the result is in there — most candidates stop after the action.

---

## 1. Bootstrapping Governance Workflows from zero — *your strongest*

**Answers:** greatest achievement · biggest challenge · owning something end to end · ambiguity

- **S** — Atlan was building a no-code governance automation platform on a new orchestration engine. There was no frontend for it.
- **T** — Architect and bootstrap it, then own conditional routing and the request task inbox.
- **A** — Built the frontend architecture from scratch against a spec JSON the engine both executed and mutated. Owned branching — up to ten branches, plus a fallback path so a request matching no condition still goes somewhere — the three approval strategies, and rule-based auto-approval. Built the inbox where requests land and approvers act.
- **R** — Shipped and live; it is how Atlan customers govern metadata changes, access and entity creation today.

**Why it scores:** zero-to-one, sustained over years, with a clear boundary between what you owned and what the backend owned. Details in [Governance Workflows](/acceldata-prep/4).

---

## 2. The orchestration layer — *your "I made a call others disagreed with"*

**Answers:** disagreement · a hard technical decision · improving how the team works · pushing back

- **S** — Every widget parsed the workflow spec itself. Fine at three widgets; not fine at the point it had grown to.
- **T** — Attribute migrations were taking days per widget and blocking a backend team that could add node types in an afternoon.
- **A** — Built one adapter between the spec document and the widget tree. Widgets take props; they no longer read the document. This cost per-widget flexibility, and not everyone agreed that was the right trade.
- **R** — Migrations went from a multi-day sweep to hours.

**Why it scores:** a real trade-off with a real cost, a decision you had to argue for, and a measurable outcome. Describe the opposing argument fairly first. Full defence of the metric in [The orchestration layer](/acceldata-prep/5).

---

## 3. The form builder that other teams adopted

**Answers:** building for other engineers · influence without authority · platform thinking

- **S** — Governance workflows needed custom forms to collect information from requesters.
- **T** — Build a form builder good enough that other teams would use it rather than roll their own.
- **A** — Six field types including one that surfaces an existing custom metadata property; drag-and-drop ordering; validation; a draft → preview → publish lifecycle; the whole thing serialised to a portable schema.
- **R** — Adopted across governance workflow modules *and* data products — teams that could have forked chose not to.

**Why it scores:** "adopted elsewhere" is the only real proof that a platform component is good. And the [no-delete decision](/acceldata-prep/7) shows domain judgement, not just component craft.

---

## 4. The bulk-operation gap — *your "what would you do differently"*

**Answers:** a mistake · what you'd change · a limitation of your own work

- **S** — Governance workflows enforce controls on metadata changes.
- **T** — They are not triggered by spreadsheet bulk updates, Playbook bulk updates, Atlan AI bulk operations, API/SDK/CLI operations, or browser-extension edits.
- **A** — The controls cover the UI path, not the programmatic ones. Your view: the right fix is enforcement at the metadata-store write path, not at each client — but that is a platform-level change, not a frontend one.
- **R** — Documented as a known limitation.

**Why it scores:** it is a real hole in your own work that you can explain precisely and have a considered opinion about, without blaming anyone. That combination is rare and managers notice it.

---

## 5. The deterministic/judgement split — *your clearest engineering opinion*

**Answers:** a recent technical decision · how you approach AI · designing for trust

- **S** — Building a background verification agent where a wrong verdict has real consequences for a real person.
- **T** — Make it reliable enough that a human reviewer can trust and audit it.
- **A** — A declared state machine on NATS events; deterministic Go pre-fetch; 17 tools keeping every rule-based decision in Go — OCR-to-form comparison across 15 document types, cross-document matching, pincode lookups, timeline and employment-gap analysis, payslip arithmetic; the model confined to one judgement step on things no rule can settle. Structured output — verdict, confidence, per-field severity — driving a reviewer console with accept / correct / raise-to-candidate.
- **R** — Every verdict is attributable to either a named rule or a single bounded judgement.

**Why it scores:** it is the most directly relevant thing you have to what Acceldata just bet the company on. Full detail in [The verification agent](/acceldata-prep/9).

---

## 6. GSoC mentoring

**Answers:** mentoring · growing others · working with people you don't manage

- **S** — Did GSoC with CircuitVerse, then returned as a mentor across two seasons.
- **T** — Guide contributors on frontend architecture and migration strategy.
- **A** — Mentored through code review and design discussion on an open-source codebase with volunteer contributors of varying experience.
- **R** — Two seasons; the work is public.

**Why it scores:** it is voluntary, it is verifiable, and it predates any job title. In a manager round that carries weight. [CircuitVerse / GSoC](/acceldata-prep/10).

---

## Coverage check

| Likely question | Story |
| --- | --- |
| Greatest achievement / proudest work | 1 |
| Hardest technical problem | 1 or 5 |
| Disagreement / had to defend a call | **2** |
| A mistake, or what you'd do differently | **4** |
| Owned something end to end | 1 |
| Built for other engineers | 3 |
| Mentoring / growing people | 6 |
| Most recent interesting work | 5 |
| Working with ambiguity | 1 |

**Gaps you should think about before Tuesday**, because none of these cover them well:

- **A conflict with a person**, not a technical disagreement. Have something real and low-drama.
- **A failure with a consequence** — something that shipped and hurt. Story 4 is a limitation, not a failure. If you have one, it is worth more than any of the above.
- **Working with a difficult stakeholder or a shifting requirement.** Governance is a compliance-adjacent product; there is almost certainly a story here about a requirement that changed late.
