learnings.title: The Bangalore question — script this one
learnings.answer:
This is the only question the recruiter flagged twice. It is also the only one where a rambling answer actively costs you the offer. Script it.

## What he told you, and what it means

> "Because you're outside Bangalore, he might ask you how desperate are you to come to Bangalore, because it shouldn't waste anybody's time, including yours and his."

Read the second half. The hiring manager is not testing enthusiasm — he is **de-risking**. He has been through candidates who interview well, get an offer, and then discover they do not actually want to move. He needs to believe the offer will not collapse at the last step.

So the answer has to be about **certainty**, not eagerness.

## Your actual position

From the call:

- You have no issue relocating. Everyone from Assam goes to Bangalore anyway.
- Your friends are all there. **You already have a place to stay.**
- The hesitation is not the city. It is full-time office work right now.

Those are three strong facts and one open question. The mistake would be leading with the open question — it makes the strong facts sound like they are softening a no.

The recruiter also said: *"No problem, I'll take care of that. I'll have a discussion with the hiring manager also."* He has already flagged it. You do not need to re-litigate it; you need to not contradict what he set up.

## The script

> "Relocating isn't an issue for me at all. I'm from Assam, and honestly most people I know from home are already in Bangalore — my friends are there, I have a place to stay, so it's not a leap into an unknown city. It's the obvious place to be for the kind of work I want to do.
>
> The only thing I wanted to understand is how the team works day to day — whether it's fully in-office, hybrid, how the Bangalore team is set up. Not because it changes my answer on moving, but because I'd rather know what I'm signing up for. What does that look like for your team?"

## Why it is built that way

- **First sentence closes the question.** "Isn't an issue for me at all" — no hedge, no conditional.
- **Then the evidence.** Friends, a place to stay, the regional norm. This is what turns a claim into a fact. *"I already have somewhere to live"* is the single most reassuring thing you can say to a manager worried about a relocation falling through.
- **Then it becomes a positive** — Bangalore is where the work is.
- **Only then, the office question** — and framed as wanting to understand the team, not as a condition. The line *"not because it changes my answer on moving"* does the work: it keeps the question from reading as a reservation.
- **Ending on a question** hands the conversation back and gets you the information you actually want.

## Things not to say

| Don't | Why |
| --- | --- |
| "I'm fine relocating, **but**…" | Everything before *but* is discarded |
| "Can I work remote?" | Turns a settled question into a negotiation, on the wrong day |
| "It depends on the compensation" | Correct, but compensation is the recruiter's conversation, not this one |
| Long explanation of why you're hesitant about office | He didn't ask. Length signals doubt |
| "I'm desperate to move to Bangalore" | Nobody believes it, and it weakens you later |

## If he pushes: "When could you start?"

That is a good sign — it means he has moved past the doubt. Have a real answer: notice period, and roughly how long the move needs. Being specific here reinforces everything above. Being vague undoes it.

## If he asks directly: "Are you okay with five days in office?"

Answer honestly, but keep it forward-looking:

> "Yes — I'd want to be in the office while I'm ramping up anyway, especially joining a team mid-way through a platform rebrand. I've worked remotely for five years and I'm productive that way, so over time I'd hope there's some flexibility, but that's not a condition for me taking the role."

That is true to your position, it does not promise something you would resent, and it does not turn the question into a negotiation.

## One thing to remember

Your recruiter is already advocating for you here — *"I'll take care of that."* The worst outcome is not that you ask about office policy. It is that you sound uncertain about moving at all, after he has told the hiring manager you are not.

learnings.title: Why Acceldata, growth expectations, and what to ask him
learnings.answer:
Three managerial questions the recruiter named — *aspiration to join Acceldata, curiosity for learning, what growth you expect* — plus the ten minutes at the end that most candidates waste.

## "Why Acceldata?"

A generic answer here is worse than no answer, because it tells him you are interviewing everywhere. Yours has three real threads. Use two.

**1. The agentic bet is the work you are already doing.**

> "You relaunched in May around autonomous agents acting on production data. The hard part of that isn't the agent — it's whether a data engineer trusts what it did. That's exactly the problem I'm on right now: an agent designed so every decision traces to either a deterministic rule or one bounded judgement, and a console where a human reviews, corrects or escalates each one. I'd rather keep working on that problem at the scale you're doing it than start something unrelated."

**2. You have spent five years on the interface over long-running backend orchestration.**

> "Everything I built at Atlan was UI over an orchestration engine the user didn't author — a workflow DAG the backend executed and mutated, rendered so the user sees their approval rather than the engine's state machine. Pipeline runs, agent actions, incidents — same shape, denser data. I know what's hard about it."

**3. The domain is one you already know.** Adjacent rather than identical — [say it precisely](/acceldata-prep/3), don't just claim it.

**What not to say:** that it is a great company, that you want to work on AI, that you are looking for a challenge. All true, all indistinguishable from every other candidate.

## "What are you looking for / what growth do you expect?"

He is checking whether he can actually offer it. Be concrete enough to be checkable, and do not pretend to want a manager title if you do not.

Honest shape, built from your own trajectory:

> "Two things. Depth — I want to own a significant surface end to end again, the way I did with Governance Workflows from zero. Short stints where you land features into someone else's architecture aren't where I do my best work.
>
> And breadth into the backend. I've been writing production Go for the last few months and I don't want to stop — frontend platform work is what I'm strongest at, but the interfaces I build sit on orchestration engines and event systems, and I'm much better at the frontend when I understand what's underneath. At an infrastructure company that seems like the right place to keep going."

Then the honest bit about title, if he raises it:

> "Title matters less to me than scope. I'd rather own something real than be called a lead over something small."

**Why the Go angle works here specifically:** Acceldata sells infrastructure. Their founders are ex-Hortonworks. A frontend engineer who deliberately went and learned the backend layer reads as someone who will be useful in more rooms — not as someone confused about their role. But be unambiguous that **frontend platform is the job you are applying for**, or you create doubt about the wrong thing.

## "How do you keep learning?"

Do not list courses. Point at evidence: the Go you learned to write production services at AICraft, the agent framework work (Eino, Bedrock, Langfuse) you picked up in months, and the fact that you have built and maintain your own study app. Concrete artefacts beat any answer about staying curious.

## Questions to ask him

Ask three or four. Each one below is grounded in something real, which is what makes them land — they prove the research without you announcing that you did research.

**On the product and the rebrand**

1. "The May launch reframes a lot around xLake. From a frontend standpoint, is the UI being rebuilt around that, or is it mostly a data-plane rebrand sitting under the existing ADOC and ADM surfaces?"
2. "The comparison page mentions ten pre-built agents with audit trails over what they do. How does the UI represent an agent's decision today, and let someone override or roll back an autonomous action — is that a solved pattern yet or still being designed?" *(This is the best question on the list. It is your exact current problem.)*

**On the engineering reality**

3. "The job posting lists React and Angular together. Is the frontend split across two frameworks for historical reasons — legacy ADOC versus newer surfaces — and is there a migration plan?" *(Direct, and he will respect that you noticed.)*
4. "The posting mentions shared components across all products, and there are now six product lines. Is there a formal design system today, or is that consolidation still in progress?"
5. "PhonePe's case study describes 1,500+ nodes monitored. What does 'real-time' mean in practice for the dashboards — and where does the frontend hit its limits on high-cardinality metrics?"
6. "Hybrid and on-prem are a named differentiator against Monte Carlo. What does that mean for the frontend — separate build and release pipelines for on-prem, or one codebase behind feature flags?"

**On the team and the role**

7. "Who owns frontend architecture for the Bangalore team — is there a Bangalore-based lead, or does direction come from Campbell?" *(Genuinely unanswerable from outside. Also tells you a lot about what the role actually is.)*
8. "Four months after the rebrand — how much of the roadmap right now is shipping the new agentic UX versus paying down debt from the rebrand?" *(Ask this one if the conversation is going well. The answer tells you what you would actually be doing.)*
9. "Is each product surface owned by its own frontend pod, or is there one team serving all of them?"

**The closing question, if it fits**

10. "What would you want the person in this role to have done by the end of their first six months?"

## The last thirty seconds

If he asks whether you have concerns, this is where you [confirm the Bangalore answer](/acceldata-prep/13) rather than reopen it. And if it has gone well, say so plainly — that you are interested, and why, in one sentence. Managers are allowed to know you want the job.
